source_text: Cedo nunc sponte de gradu isto. Omnibus dictum sit, Quaerite et invenietis; tamen et hic expetit sensus certare cum interpretationis gubernaculo. Nulla vox divina ita dissoluta est et diffusa, ut verba tantum defendantur, et ratio verborum non constituatur. Sed in primis hoc propono, unum itaque et certum aliquid institutum esse a Christo quod credere omni modo debeant nationes, et idcirco quaerere, ut possint, cum invenerint, credere. Unius porro et certi instituti infinita inquisitio non potest esse. Quaerendum est, donec invenias, et credendum, ubi inveneris, et nihil amplius, nisi custodiendum quod credidisti, dum hoc insuper. credas, aliud non esse credendum, ideoque nec requirendum, cum id inveneris et credideris quod ab eo institutum est qui non aliud tibi mandat inquirendum quam quod instituit. De hoc quidem si qui dubitat, constabit penes nos esse id quod a Christo institutum est. Interim ex fiducia probationis praevenio, admonens quosdam nihil esse quaerendum ultra quae crediderunt id esse quod quaerere debuerunt, ne, Quaerite et invenietis, sine disciplina rationis interpretentur.
thought_title: The limit of seeking: believe what Christ instituted, then seek nothing further
orientation: Tertullian is beginning his argument that the command 'Seek and you will find' has a fixed limit, namely the doctrine Christ instituted, which once found and believed leaves nothing further to seek.
pass_a_gloss: Come now, of my own accord from that step. Let it have been said to all, Seek and you will find; nevertheless here too the sense demands to contend with the helm of interpretation. No divine utterance is so loose and scattered that only the words are defended, and the reason of the words is not established. But first of all I propose this, that one and therefore certain something has been instituted by Christ which the nations ought by all means to believe, and for that reason to seek, so that they may be able, when they have found it, to believe. Moreover of one and certain institution there cannot be an endless inquiry. It must be sought until you find, and believed where you have found, and nothing more, except that what you have believed must be guarded, while you believe this in addition, that another thing is not to be believed, and therefore not to be sought again, when you have found and believed that which has been instituted by him who commands you to seek nothing other than what he instituted. About this indeed if anyone doubts, it will be established that among us is that which has been instituted by Christ. Meanwhile from the confidence of proof I go ahead, warning certain people that nothing is to be sought beyond what they have believed, that that is what they ought to have sought, lest they interpret Seek and you will find without the discipline of reason.

choices.why: The metaphor of steering interpretation; 'helm' keeps the nautical image of control and direction.
Tertullian contrasts loose, scattered words with fixed meaning; 'loose' preserves the sense of lacking cohesion.
The logical ground or rationale behind the words; 'reason' captures the argumentative force Tertullian demands.
Tertullian uses this term for the seeking activity; 'inquiry' is neutral and matches the legal-philosophical register.
The gerundive expresses obligation; 'guarded' preserves the defensive, protective sense of keeping the deposit.
The phrase pairs disciplina with ratio; 'discipline of reason' keeps both the ordered training and the rational method Tertullian insists on.

pass_b_english: Now let me step down from that position of my own accord. Let it be said to everyone, “Seek and you will find” (Matthew 7:7); yet even here the meaning demands to be settled by the helm of interpretation. No divine utterance is so loose and scattered that only the words are defended and the reason of the words is not established. But first of all I lay this down: that one definite and certain thing was instituted by Christ which the nations must believe in every way, and that they must seek for this reason, so that when they have found it they may believe. Moreover, there cannot be an endless inquiry into one definite and certain institution. You must seek until you find, and believe when you have found, and nothing more, except to guard what you have believed—while you believe this further, that nothing else is to be believed, and therefore nothing else is to be sought again, once you have found and believed what was instituted by him who commands you to seek nothing other than what he instituted. If anyone doubts about this, it will be established that what was instituted by Christ is with us. In the meantime, out of confidence in the proof, I go ahead and warn certain people that nothing is to be sought beyond what they have believed—that this is what they ought to have sought—lest they interpret “Seek and you will find” without the discipline of reason.
